etymology: Translation of Hebrew mo’adim (singular mo’ed), from the root yā’ad, to appoint or designate by agreement. The term appears first in Genesis 1:14 where God appoints the celestial bodies for “signs and appointed times” — establishing from creation that time itself is divinely ordered, not cyclically indifferent. Leviticus 23:2 applies the term specifically to the sacred calendar of Israel: the mo’adim are the times God appoints for covenant assembly, worship, and commemoration. The English “appointed times” or “feasts of the LORD” preserves the sense of divine initiative: these are not Israel's feasts but the LORD's.
biblical_def: The appointed times are the sacred seasons that the LORD commanded Israel to observe as covenant assemblies throughout the agricultural and liturgical year — collectively defined in Leviticus 23, Numbers 28–29, and Deuteronomy 16. They include the weekly Sabbath (Lev 23:3), the Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread (Lev 23:5–8), the Feast of Firstfruits (Lev 23:9–14), the Feast of Weeks / Pentecost (Lev 23:15–22), the Feast of Trumpets / Rosh Hashanah (Lev 23:23–25), the Day of Atonement / Yom Kippur (Lev 23:26–32), and the Feast of Tabernacles / Sukkot (Lev 23:33–43). The LORD identifies them explicitly as “My feasts” (Lev 23:2) — not Israel's religious calendar but the LORD's own appointments within the covenant year. Each feast carries a dual character: it commemorates a historical redemptive event (the Exodus, the wilderness journey, the giving of the law at Sinai) and anticipates a future redemptive fulfillment. This is the typological structure Paul identifies in Colossians 2:17: the feasts are “a shadow of what is to come; but the substance belongs to Christ.” The shadow is real — it was divinely appointed and demanded faithful observance — but the substance that casts the shadow is Christ Himself, whose life, death, resurrection, ascension, and coming return fulfill every feast's anticipatory content. The three pilgrimage feasts (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles) required every Israelite male to appear before the LORD at the central sanctuary (Deut 16:16) — a tri-annual covenant renewal anchoring the community's common life in the LORD's presence.
webster_summary: The appointed times (mo’adim) are the sacred seasons prescribed in Leviticus 23 as the LORD's covenant calendar — seven annual feasts plus the weekly Sabbath — each commemorating past redemptive acts and typologically anticipating their fulfillment in the life and work of Jesus Christ.
webster_full: APPOINTED TIMES. Hebrew mo’adim (singular mo’ed), from yā’ad, to appoint: the sacred seasons the LORD prescribed for covenant Israel in Leviticus 23 and Numbers 28–29, comprehending the weekly Sabbath and seven annual feast-cycles marking the agricultural and liturgical year.

2. The seven annual mo’adim: (1) Passover / Pesach (Nisan 14); (2) Unleavened Bread / Chag HaMatzot (Nisan 15–21); (3) Firstfruits / Bikkurim (first Sunday after Passover); (4) Weeks / Shavuot / Pentecost (fifty days after Firstfruits); (5) Trumpets / Rosh Hashanah (Tishri 1); (6) Atonement / Yom Kippur (Tishri 10); (7) Tabernacles / Sukkot (Tishri 15–22). Collectively they rehearse the entire arc of redemption in annual cycle.

3. Christological fulfillment (Col 2:17): Passover fulfilled in Christ's crucifixion (1 Cor 5:7); Firstfruits in His resurrection (1 Cor 15:20); Pentecost in the Spirit's outpouring (Acts 2); Atonement in the priestly self-offering (Heb 9:11–12). Trumpets and Tabernacles await final eschatological fulfillment in the second coming and eternal habitation of God with His people.

4. The LORD's ownership: Leviticus 23:2, 4 declares “My feasts” and “feasts of the LORD” — the covenant calendar belongs to God, not to Israel's cultural preference. Observance was obligatory, not optional; non-observance of the Sabbath and pilgrimage feasts carried covenant-curse consequences.

5. New covenant status (Col 2:16–17; Heb 10:1): the substance having come, the shadows are not obligatory on the church. The Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15) and Paul's letters (Gal 4:10; Rom 14:5–6) establish that Gentile believers are not bound to the Mosaic festival calendar, though the typological richness of the feasts remains instructive for understanding the fullness of Christ's redemptive work.

corruption_summary: The appointed times have been corrupted in two directions: by Judaizing movements that impose Mosaic festival observance on the New Testament church as a condition of spiritual maturity, and by Gentile Christianity's wholesale abandonment of the feasts' typological-theological richness, leaving believers without the annual redemptive-historical rehearsal Christ Himself fulfilled at the precise moments each feast anticipated.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrew Roots and Messianic Judaizing movements have reversed the apostolic settlement of Acts 15 and Galatians 4 by requiring Gentile believers to observe the Mosaic calendar as a marker of authentic discipleship and covenant standing. This is precisely the Galatian error Paul calls a return to bondage (Gal 4:9–10). Colossians 2:16 explicitly forbids judging one another over festivals, new moons, or Sabbaths that were shadows; the substance has arrived. The mo’adim were divinely commanded and precious in their appointed season, but their covenant-obligatory force was fulfilled and therefore terminated by the coming of Christ. To reimpose them is not to recover biblical depth but to deny that the substance has come.

The opposite corruption is the evangelical church's poverty-of-ignorance regarding the feasts: treating the Old Testament's liturgical calendar as irrelevant religious history rather than as the typological grammar by which the New Testament's greatest doctrines (incarnation, atonement, resurrection, Pentecost, second coming) are properly understood. A church that has never learned to read Passover is a church that will preach a thinner gospel than Scripture's own. The solution is not to reinstate the feasts as obligatory but to teach their Christological content — to let the shadows teach the shadow's meaning — so that every Good Friday becomes richer because it is understood as Passover fulfilled, and every Pentecost Sunday becomes the outpouring of Shavuot's harvest.
roots_summary: The appointed times root in creation's ordered time (Gen 1:14), in the Exodus commemoration (Passover as the covenant-forming event), in the Sinai legislation (Lev 23; Num 28–29; Deut 16), and in the prophetic eschatological vision of all nations streaming to Jerusalem for the final Feast of Tabernacles (Zech 14:16).
roots_lines: Creation time-order — Gen 1:14: the sun and moon appointed for “signs and appointed times” (mo’adim); the sacred calendar is embedded in the created order of light and time itself, not imposed arbitrarily on history

Exodus Passover — Exod 12: the founding mo’ed from which all others derive; the LORD's deliverance of Israel from Egypt is the paradigm for all subsequent redemptive acts and the primary content of the covenant calendar's memorial structure
Sinai legislation — Lev 23; Num 28–29; Deut 16: the full codification of the seven annual feasts plus the weekly Sabbath as the LORD's comprehensive covenant calendar for Israel in the land

Prophetic eschatology — Zech 14:16–19; Isa 66:23: the feast-structure projected forward into the eschatological age when all nations will worship the King and the entire cosmos will observe the final Sabbath rest

Colossians 2:16–17 and Hebrews 8–10: the New Testament's interpretive key — shadow vs. substance; the feasts were real, divinely appointed, and instructive; their covenant-obligatory force is fulfilled and their typological content is now fully visible in Christ
usage: The annual rehearsal of the appointed times gave covenant Israel a structured theological education: each feast cycle re-told the story of redemption, re-enacted the pattern of deliverance, and re-oriented the community toward its future hope. The church that learns to read the mo’adim gains this same structural richness for understanding the full architecture of redemption — creation, fall, exodus, Sinai, atonement, Pentecost, and consummation — rehearsed in annual typological sequence.

The three pilgrimage feasts (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles) required every male Israelite to appear before the LORD at the central sanctuary — the covenant community physically gathered at the divine presence. The New Testament fulfills this pattern in the church's weekly gathering before the risen Christ (“where two or three are gathered”, Matt 18:20) and ultimately in the New Jerusalem where the LORD God Almighty is the temple (Rev 21:22).

Colossians 2:17 — “the substance belongs to Christ” — is the key that unlocks typological reading of the entire appointed-times calendar. The Christian reads the feasts not as obsolete laws but as revelatory previews: Passover is the cross; Firstfruits is the resurrection; Pentecost is the Spirit's coming; Atonement is the priestly intercession; Tabernacles is the coming eternal dwelling of God with His people. Every feast teaches something about the Christ who came and the Christ who comes.

etymology: New (Old English neowe, from Proto-Germanic *neuja, fresh, recent) + covenant (from Old French covenant, agreement, from Latin convenire, to come together) + signs (Old English signe, from Latin signum, mark, token, seal). The phrase designates the two ordinances of the new covenant — baptism and the Lord's Supper — that Christ instituted as visible, enacted proclamations of His death, burial, resurrection, and coming return. The older term “sacraments” is used in the Westminster and Reformed traditions; the Baptist tradition (following the 1689 LBCF) prefers “ordinances” to emphasize their commanded, instituted character without implying the ex opere operato transmission of grace taught by Rome.
biblical_def: The new covenant signs are the two ordinances Christ instituted for His church to be practiced throughout the age between His ascension and return: baptism (Matt 28:19–20; Rom 6:3–4; Col 2:12) and the Lord's Supper (Matt 26:26–28; 1 Cor 11:23–26). Both are visible enactments of the gospel: baptism proclaims the believer's union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Rom 6:4); the Supper proclaims the Lord's death until He comes (1 Cor 11:26). As new-covenant signs they fulfill and supersede the old-covenant signs of circumcision and Passover: circumcision pointed to the cutting off of the old man, now accomplished in Spirit-baptism (Col 2:11–12); Passover proclaimed the lamb's death for the redemption of the people, now accomplished in Christ (1 Cor 5:7). The 1689 LBCF (28.1) defines baptism as “an ordinance of the New Testament, ordained by Jesus Christ, to be unto the party baptized, a sign of his fellowship with him, in his death and resurrection.” The Supper (1689 LBCF 30.1) is “a memorial of his suffering and death” through which Christ's people “feed upon his body and blood to their spiritual nourishment and growth in grace.” The two signs together form the gospel-in-embodied-form: the death and resurrection proclaimed in water and bread and cup, making visible to the watching congregation what the preached Word declares to the listening ear. Neither sign is a mere formality; both are means of grace through which the Spirit nourishes the faith of genuine believers who receive them in faith.
webster_summary: The new covenant signs are the two ordinances Christ instituted for His church — believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper — as visible enactments of the gospel that proclaim His death, burial, resurrection, and coming return throughout the age between His ascension and return.
webster_full: NEW COVENANT SIGNS. The two ordinances instituted by Christ for His church as visible, enacted signs of the new covenant: (1) Baptism, the immersion of the confessing believer into water in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19), proclaiming union with Christ in His death and resurrection (Rom 6:4); (2) The Lord's Supper, the partaking of bread and cup in remembrance of Christ's body and blood, proclaiming His death until He comes (1 Cor 11:26).

2. Both signs are visual Gospel: where the preached Word addresses the ear, the ordinances address the eye and touch — baptism enacts burial and resurrection; the Supper enacts reception of Christ's atoning sacrifice. Together they form the complete sensory proclamation of the gospel in embodied form.

3. Old-to-new typological continuity: circumcision (Gen 17; Col 2:11–12) anticipates Spirit-baptism and is superseded by water-baptism in the new covenant; Passover (Exod 12; 1 Cor 5:7) anticipates the Supper and is superseded by the breaking of bread in Christ's death. The signs change; the covenant grace signified is the same.

4. The Baptist position (1689 LBCF 28–30): believer's baptism by immersion as the New Testament pattern (Matt 3:16; Acts 8:38); the Supper as memorial and spiritual feast, not propitiatory sacrifice or transubstantiation; both ordinances restricted to the baptized membership of the local church.

5. Neither sign conveys grace automatically (contra Rome's ex opere operato); both are means through which the Spirit acts upon the faith of genuine believers. Receiving either sign in hypocrisy or unbelief is a sin against the Lord's body (1 Cor 11:27–29), not a guarantee of grace.

corruption_summary: The new covenant signs have been corrupted by Rome's sacramentalism (signs that automatically confer grace, including baptismal regeneration and the Mass as a re-sacrifice), by Protestant sacramentarianism (signs so reduced to mere memorial that the Spirit's real action through them is denied), and by paedobaptist confusion of the sign with the regenerate covenant community.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman Catholic sacramentology corrupts both signs: baptism becomes the instrument of regeneration itself (baptismal regeneration), not the sign of a regeneration already worked by the Spirit through the Word; the Supper becomes a propitiatory re-sacrifice of Christ in the Mass (transubstantiation), not a proclamation of the completed and unrepeatable sacrifice. Both errors elevate the sign above or into the thing signified, collapsing the distinction between the visible enactment and the invisible grace. The Reformation's recovery of the distinction — the sign is real, the grace is real, but they are not identical — is the essential correction.

Reformed paedobaptism commits a different confusion: applying the covenant-sign of baptism to the infants of believers on the grounds that they are members of the covenant community. The 1689 LBCF's position — grounded in the believer's confession of faith as the prerequisite for the baptism-sign — is that the new covenant is explicitly a covenant of regenerate members (Jer 31:33–34; Heb 8:11: “they shall all know me”), and therefore the sign of new-covenant membership belongs only to those who confess the faith that marks new-covenant inclusion. The issue is not whether children are precious and to be nurtured in the faith — they are — but whether the sign anticipates regeneration (paedobaptism) or follows and attests it (credobaptism). Scripture's pattern throughout Acts is confess-then-baptize, not baptize-then-hope-for-faith.
roots_summary: The new covenant signs root in the old covenant's typological signs (circumcision pointing to heart-circumcision; Passover pointing to the Lamb's sacrifice), in Christ's institution of both at His baptism and in the upper room, and in the apostolic practice codified in Matthew 28, Romans 6, and 1 Corinthians 10–11.
roots_lines: Old-covenant anticipation — Gen 17 (circumcision); Exod 12 (Passover): the two primary old-covenant signs whose spiritual content is what baptism and the Supper carry forward in fulfilled, clearer form in the new covenant age

Christ's institution of baptism — Matt 28:19–20: the Great Commission formula establishes baptism in the Trinitarian name as the entrance sign of discipleship; Acts records its immediate apostolic practice (Acts 2:38; 8:38; 10:47–48)

Christ's institution of the Supper — Matt 26:26–29; 1 Cor 11:23–25: the upper room words of institution (“this is my body... this is my blood of the covenant”) establish the Supper as the covenant-renewal meal of the new covenant community

Apostolic theology of baptism — Rom 6:3–4; Col 2:12; Gal 3:27: the sign of burial and resurrection; union with Christ's death and the newness of resurrection life; not the ground of justification but its visible proclamation

Apostolic theology of the Supper — 1 Cor 10:16–17; 11:26–29: the cup of blessing as participation in Christ's blood; the bread as participation in His body; the Supper as the community's proclamation of the Lord's death until He comes
usage: First Corinthians 11:26 identifies the Lord's Supper as an act of proclamation: “you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes.” This frames the ordinance not as private spiritual nourishment only but as a communal declaration addressed to the gathered church and, by extension, to the watching world. Every Supper is a sermon in bread and cup.

Romans 6:4 grounds the call to walk in newness of life directly in the baptism-sign: we were “buried with Him through baptism into death” so that we might walk in resurrection-newness. Baptism is not merely a ceremony of church membership; it is the enacted declaration of a death and resurrection that has already occurred in union with Christ — the basis of the entire sanctification ethic of Romans 6–8.

The two ordinances together function as the gospel's embodied form within the local church's life: baptism marks entry into the covenant community; the Supper marks ongoing covenant renewal. A church that treats both as optional or infrequent loses the embodied gospel-structure that Christ designed for the community's weekly and occasional life together.

etymology: Pilgrimage (Middle English pilgrimage, from Old French pelrinage, from pelerin, pilgrim, ultimately from Latin peregrinus, foreigner or traveler) + feasts (Old English fæsten, festival, from Latin festum). The pilgrimage feasts translate Hebrew shalosh regalim (literally, “three foot-journeys”), referring to the three annual occasions on which all adult male Israelites were required to travel on foot to the central sanctuary to appear before the LORD. The term also translates chag (festival, celebration), the Hebrew word specifically for the three major feasts involving the whole assembly.
biblical_def: The pilgrimage feasts are the three annual covenant assemblies at which God commanded all adult male Israelites to appear before the LORD at the central sanctuary: the Feast of Unleavened Bread / Passover (Pesach, in the spring, marking the Exodus), the Feast of Weeks / Pentecost (Shavuot, fifty days after Firstfruits, marking the grain harvest and the Sinai covenant-giving), and the Feast of Tabernacles / Booths (Sukkot, in the autumn, marking the wilderness sojourn). Deuteronomy 16:16 states the mandate: “Three times a year all your males shall appear before the LORD your God in the place which He chooses: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Tabernacles; and they shall not appear before the LORD empty-handed.” The physical pilgrimage was an enacted theology: Israel was a people on the move, bound for the presence of God, bringing the firstfruits of labor as a visible declaration that all provision came from the LORD's hand. Psalm 84:7 captures the pilgrim spirit: “They go from strength to strength — every one of them appears before God in Zion.” Each feast bore a specific Christological anticipation: Passover pointed to the cross (1 Cor 5:7); Pentecost to the Spirit's outpouring (Acts 2:1–4); Tabernacles to the final dwelling of God with His people (Rev 21:3). Zechariah 14:16 projects the Feast of Tabernacles into the eschatological age when all nations will stream to Jerusalem to worship the King.
webster_summary: The pilgrimage feasts (shalosh regalim) are the three annual covenant assemblies — Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles — at which all adult male Israelites were required to appear before the LORD at the central sanctuary, each bearing firstfruits and anticipating a specific dimension of Christ's redemptive work.
webster_full: PILGRIMAGE FEASTS. Hebrew shalosh regalim, the three annual “foot-journeys” mandated by Mosaic covenant law (Exod 23:14–17; 34:22–23; Deut 16:16) at which all Israelite males were required to appear before the LORD: (1) Passover / Unleavened Bread (spring; commemorating the Exodus); (2) Weeks / Pentecost (early summer; commemorating the Sinai covenant and the grain harvest); (3) Tabernacles / Booths (autumn; commemorating the wilderness sojourn).

2. The “not empty-handed” requirement (Deut 16:16–17): each pilgrim brought an offering proportional to his blessing. The feast was simultaneously a covenant-renewal assembly, a memorial rehearsal, and a thanksgiving acknowledgment that all provision was the LORD's. The empty-handed worshiper was not a worshiper at all.

3. Christological fulfillment: Passover → the crucifixion (“Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us,” 1 Cor 5:7); Pentecost → the Spirit's outpouring inaugurating the new covenant (Acts 2:1–4; the disciples were gathered for Shavuot when the Spirit came); Tabernacles → the incarnation (“the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us,” John 1:14) and the final eschatological dwelling (Rev 21:3).

4. The Psalms of Ascent (Ps 120–134) were the pilgrimage hymns sung as worshipers traveled to Jerusalem — a liturgical soundtrack for the journey to the divine presence. The pilgrim theology of these psalms (trust on the road, joy at arrival, dependence throughout) shapes the New Testament's description of the Christian life as a pilgrimage toward the city whose builder and maker is God (Heb 11:10).

5. Eschatological fulfillment (Zech 14:16): all nations will keep the Feast of Tabernacles in the age to come — the local, annual, Israel-centered pilgrimage universalized into the eternal worship of the King. The three foot-journeys of the covenant calendar become the single eternal journey of the redeemed into the presence of God.

corruption_summary: The pilgrimage feasts have been corrupted by historical-critical reduction to agricultural folk religion and by evangelical neglect that strips the covenant calendar of its typological richness, leaving believers without the annual redemptive-historical rehearsal Christ Himself fulfilled at the precise moments each feast anticipated.
corruption_paragraphs: Wellhausen's critical developmental scheme treated the pilgrimage feasts as Israel's adaptation of ancient Canaanite agricultural festivals — the religious calendar as cultural borrowing rather than divine institution. On this account, Passover was originally a nomadic shepherd's spring rite; Pentecost a grain harvest festival; Tabernacles an autumnal fruit festival. The Moses and Sinai narrative came later to give them an Israelite historical veneer. This entire reconstruction is methodologically committed to denying divine institution and typological intentionality. The Reformed confessional position holds that the Mosaic legislation of Exodus 23, Leviticus 23, and Deuteronomy 16 is exactly what it claims to be: the LORD's direct command organizing Israel's covenant year around three divinely appointed memorial assemblies at the place He chose.

The evangelical church's neglect is subtler but equally impoverishing: treating the pilgrimage feasts as Old Testament history completed and therefore irrelevant to the church's theological life. The result is a Gospel proclaimed without the typological grammar that Scripture itself uses to explain it: without Passover, the Lord's Supper loses its Exodus-and-redemption resonance; without Pentecost, Acts 2 loses its harvest-and-covenant-giving depth; without Tabernacles, the incarnation (John 1:14) and the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:3) lose their dwelling-of-God-with-people texture. The feasts are not the church's required observance; they are the church's required curriculum.
roots_summary: The pilgrimage feasts root in the Mosaic covenant legislation of Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy; in the Psalms of Ascent as the liturgical soundtrack of the pilgrimage tradition; and in the New Testament's explicit fulfillment of each feast at the precise salvific moments of Christ's death, resurrection, and the Spirit's coming.
roots_lines: Exodus 23:14–17; 34:22–23 — the original pilgrimage mandate: three times yearly before the LORD; the annual covenant-renewal rhythm embedded in the Mosaic law from Sinai
Deuteronomy 16:1–17 — the full pilgrimage legislation for the land: Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles detailed with the not-empty-handed requirement; the central sanctuary as the locus of the LORD's name

Psalms of Ascent (Ps 120–134) — the pilgrimage hymnbook: fifteen psalms sung on the ascent to Jerusalem; the entire pilgrimage spirituality of trust, longing, joy, dependence, and arrival compressed into a fifteen-psalm arc

New Testament fulfillment moments: Passover → crucifixion (1 Cor 5:7); Pentecost → Spirit (Acts 2); Tabernacles → incarnation (John 1:14) and eschatological dwelling (Rev 21:3) — each feast met by the event it anticipated at precisely the calendar moment

Zechariah 14:16 — eschatological universalization: the three-annual Israel-only requirement becomes the eternal all-nations worship of the King; the pilgrimage feasts point forward to the final and permanent assembly of all the redeemed before God
usage: The not-empty-handed principle of Deuteronomy 16:17 — “Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD your God which He has given you” — is the covenantal logic behind New Testament proportional giving (2 Cor 9:7: “each one must give as he has made up his mind”). The pilgrim who arrives at the feast bringing nothing has acknowledged no blessing and given no worship; the pilgrim who arrives in proportion to his blessing has made a concrete theological statement about the source of his provision.

The Psalms of Ascent (Ps 120–134) provide a liturgical theology of pilgrimage: the worshiper begins in distress (Ps 120), moves through trust in the keeper of Israel who neither slumbers nor sleeps (Ps 121), ascends in joy to the house of the LORD (Ps 122), waits on the LORD's mercy (Ps 123), trusts in the LORD's protection of His people (Ps 125), and arrives in the unity and blessing of the assembled congregation (Ps 133–134). The church's weekly gathering recapitulates this pilgrimage arc in miniature.

The fulfillment of each pilgrimage feast at the precise calendar moment of the event it anticipated is one of Scripture's most astonishing evidential patterns: Jesus died as the Passover lambs were being slaughtered; rose as the Firstfruits were being waved; the Spirit came on the day of Pentecost. The calendar is not coincidence; it is God's design, written into the Mosaic law centuries before the events it anticipated, demonstrating that the entire sacrificial and festal system was a divinely authored script for the drama of redemption.

etymology: Holy (Old English halig, set apart, consecrated, whole; cognate with German heilig; the concept of sacred separation and dedication to God) + convocation (from Latin convocatio, a calling together, from convocare: con-, together + vocare, to call). The phrase translates Hebrew miqra’ qōdesh (miqra’, something called out or a sacred assembly, from qara’, to call; qōdesh, holiness or the set-apart state). The term appears first in Leviticus 23:2–4 as the defining character of Israel's appointed feasts: they are not self-organized gatherings but divinely called assemblies.
biblical_def: The holy convocation (miqra’ qōdesh) is the assembly that God calls out from the ordinary course of life for the purpose of covenant worship — a gathering whose authority, timing, and character derive from God's call rather than human initiative. Leviticus 23:2 introduces the entire appointed-times calendar with this designation: the mo’adim are “holy convocations” — times at which Israel is not merely invited but called, as a community, into the LORD's presence for a set purpose. The weekly Sabbath is explicitly named a “holy convocation” (Lev 23:3), establishing the pattern from the most regular assembly to the most solemn annual one. Each major feast — the first and last days of Unleavened Bread (Lev 23:7–8), Pentecost (Num 28:26), Trumpets (Lev 23:24), Atonement (Lev 23:27), and the first and eighth days of Tabernacles (Lev 23:35, 36) — is a holy convocation. The holy convocation required “no customary work” (Num 28:18) — the ordinary labor of the week is suspended because God has called the community out of that ordinary into something extraordinary. Isaiah 1:13 records the LORD's rebuke of corrupt convocations: “Bring no more futile sacrifices; incense is an abomination to Me. The New Moons, the Sabbaths, and the calling of assemblies — I cannot endure iniquity and the sacred meeting.” This verse establishes a critical principle: the holy convocation is desecrated when the assembly brings iniquity with it. The form without the reality of covenant fidelity becomes an abomination. The New Testament fulfillment of the holy convocation is the church's weekly gathering in Christ's name (Matt 18:20; Heb 10:25) — a community called out of the world by the risen Christ, in whose presence the assembly meets.
webster_summary: The holy convocation (miqra’ qōdesh) is the divinely called assembly of the covenant community, mandated at each appointed feast and the weekly Sabbath, in which Israel was called out of ordinary life into the presence of the LORD for worship, remembrance, and covenant renewal.
webster_full: HOLY CONVOCATION. Hebrew miqra’ qōdesh: a divinely called sacred assembly; the designation given to the weekly Sabbath and to the opening and closing days of each major feast in the Mosaic covenant calendar (Lev 23:3, 7, 8, 21, 24, 27, 35, 36; Num 28:18, 25, 26).

2. The name is theologically programmatic: miqra’ (from qara’, to call or summon) means the assembly is constituted by God's call, not the people's convenience or decision. The New Testament church's name ekklēsia (called-out ones) is the direct Greek equivalent — the community defined by the divine summons that brought it into being.

3. The no-customary-work prohibition: each holy convocation suspended ordinary labor (Num 28:18, 25, 26; Lev 23:3, 7–8) — the economic world was set aside because God had called the community to something that relativized all ordinary priorities. Work will resume; the holy convocation will not recur until the next appointed time.

4. Isaiah 1:13 — the corrupted convocation: God rejects convocations that bring iniquity with them. The assembly that maintains all the correct forms while harboring unrepentant covenant unfaithfulness becomes an abomination rather than a holy convocation. The form of gathered worship is not automatically holy; it becomes holy when it is the genuine response of a community whose heart is toward the LORD.

5. New Testament fulfillment: the church is the eschatological holy convocation — the called-out community (Matt 16:18; Acts 2:47) that gathers in Christ's name (Matt 18:20), under His priestly presidency (Heb 8:1–2), for Word and ordinance. Hebrews 10:25 makes the weekly assembly a moral obligation: “not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together.”

Lev 23:3

corruption_summary: The holy convocation has been corrupted in modern evangelical practice by the consumer-church model that replaces the divinely called assembly with an audience-experience — transforming the miqra’ qōdesh from a covenant obligation of the community to an optional personal enrichment event for individual spiritual consumers.
corruption_paragraphs: The ancient corruption is Isaiah's: attending the form of the sacred assembly while bringing iniquity with it — the Sabbath observed externally while the heart pursues exploitation and injustice (Isa 58:3–7). God rejects this convocation as more offensive than no convocation at all (Isa 1:13–15). The modern church faces the same corruption in multiple guises: the congregation that maintains worship services while tolerating unrepentant sin in its membership; the church that holds theologically correct forms while its leadership harbors pride and self-aggrandizement; the worship gathering that performs the externals of reverence while the congregation's hearts are far from God (Isa 29:13). The miqra’ qōdesh demands not only the form of assembly but the reality of a community that has come clean before the LORD.

The more modern corruption is the dissolution of assembly itself into a consumer experience. The theological category of holy convocation is a called-out, gathered, covenantal community with obligations to each other and to the Lord of the assembly. The consumer-church model reconstitutes this as an audience that attends performances and exits without covenant bonds. “Forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) becomes normalized; the covenant community's weekly gathering is replaced by personal spiritual content consumed on individual schedules. The church is not an audience God addresses; it is a covenant people God assembles.
roots_summary: The holy convocation roots in Israel's covenant-assembly pattern throughout the wilderness (Numbers 10's trumpet-summoned assemblies) and the Mosaic feast-calendar (Lev 23), in the Psalms of Ascent as the pilgrimage-assembly spirituality, and in the New Testament church as the eschatological fulfillment of the called-out covenant community.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqra’ (from qara’, to call or summon): the assembly constituted by divine call, not human organization; its authority derives from the One who summons, not the organizational capacity of the gathered

Numbers 10:1–10 — the silver trumpet protocol: God commands Moses to make two silver trumpets for summoning the assembly and for signaling the march; the trumpet-call is God's initiative calling Israel out of their tents into the covenant gathering

Leviticus 23 — the feast-calendar as the annual schedule of holy convocations: seven assemblies plus the weekly Sabbath, each marked by cessation of ordinary labor and gathering for the LORD's appointed purpose

Psalms 84 and 122 — the assembly-longing psalms: “How lovely is Your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts!” (Ps 84:1); “I was glad when they said to me, let us go into the house of the LORD” (Ps 122:1); the affective dimension of holy convocation — not duty alone but delight

New Testament ekklēsia — Matt 16:18; 18:20; Acts 2:42–47: the church as the eschatological holy convocation; constituted by Christ's call, gathered in His name, under His priestly mediation, for Word and ordinance and mutual covenant care
usage: The theological weight of Leviticus 23:2 — “these are My feasts” — transfers directly to the New Testament church's Lord's Day assembly. The gathered church does not belong to the pastor, to the congregation's preference, or to the broader culture's scheduling calendar; it is the LORD's holy convocation, shaped by His agenda, under His authority, for the purpose He has appointed.

Isaiah 1:13's rebuke of corrupted convocations provides the diagnostic question for every gathered church: does the assembly actually bring the community into the presence of a holy God for genuine covenant renewal, or does it bring the forms of worship as a covering for covenant unfaithfulness? The corrupted convocation is worse than no convocation — it is presumption made liturgical. Church discipline and congregational accountability are the institutional safeguards that maintain the difference between a holy convocation and a religious performance.

Hebrews 10:25 — “not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” — is the New Testament's direct application of the holy-convocation principle to the church's weekly Lord's Day gathering. The verse does not say “not merely reducing the frequency of your attendance”; it says “not forsaking,” a verb used in Hebrews for the abandonment of a covenant commitment. The weekly assembly is not a spiritual enhancement option; it is the covenant community's regular constitutive act.

etymology: Believer (from Old English gelyfan, to believe; one who places trust and confidence in a specific object or person) + baptism (Greek baptisma, from baptizō, to immerse, dip, or plunge). The phrase “believer's baptism” or credobaptism (from Latin credo, I believe) is the distinctive Baptist and Reformed Baptist teaching that water baptism in the name of the Trinity is properly administered only to those who make a credible confession of faith in Jesus Christ — not to infants or the unbaptized who have not yet confessed. The term emerged in polemical contrast to paedobaptism during the sixteenth-century Reformation debates.
biblical_def: Believer's baptism is the doctrine that water baptism is the New Testament's proper first act of obedience for one who has repented, believed, and confessed Jesus Christ as Lord — the enacted declaration of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, administered by immersion in water in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Acts pattern is consistently confess-then-baptize: Peter's Pentecost sermon ends with “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38); the Ethiopian eunuch confesses “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God” before Philip baptizes him (Acts 8:37–38). The theological ground is Romans 6:3–4: baptism enacts a death to the old life and a resurrection into the new, a transition that only a regenerate person can honestly confess to have undergone. Galatians 3:27 declares that “all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” — the clothing-language presupposes a prior reality (union with Christ through faith) that the baptism publicly enacts. The 1689 LBCF (29.2) is explicit: “None are to be baptized, but such as do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ.” Believer's baptism is thus not merely a different mode debate (immersion vs. sprinkling) but a different understanding of what the sign signifies and to whom it belongs: it belongs to the regenerate covenant community of the new covenant, whose members all know the Lord (Jer 31:34; Heb 8:11).
webster_summary: Believer's baptism (credobaptism) is the doctrine that water baptism is properly administered only to those who confess repentance and faith in Jesus Christ — as the enacted sign of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, following the consistent Acts pattern of confession-before-baptism.
webster_full: BELIEVER'S BAPTISM. Also credobaptism (L. credo, I believe): the doctrine that Christian water baptism belongs properly and exclusively to those who make a credible confession of repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, because the sign represents a spiritual death and resurrection already accomplished by the Spirit through the regenerating Word.

2. The Acts pattern: (1) Peter's Pentecost sermon — repent, then be baptized (Acts 2:38); (2) Philip and the eunuch — if you believe with all your heart, you may be baptized (Acts 8:37); (3) Cornelius's household — received the Spirit first, then baptized (Acts 10:44–48); (4) Lydia — the Lord opened her heart, then her household was baptized (Acts 16:15). In every clear case the sequence is: God's saving work first, baptism as the responsive enacted confession second.

3. The new covenant logic (Jer 31:33–34; Heb 8:10–11): the new covenant, unlike the old, is characterized by universal inward knowledge of the Lord among all its members (“they shall all know me”). The covenant community is a regenerate community; its sign belongs to the regenerate.

4. The paedobaptist counter and the credobaptist response: paedobaptism applies the sign on the basis of covenant membership in a mixed community (as circumcision applied to Isaac before faith). Credobaptism holds that the new covenant has categorically different membership criteria — inward regeneration rather than physical descent — and therefore a categorically different sign protocol.

5. The 1689 LBCF position (29.1–2): believer's baptism by immersion is the New Testament pattern; it is not a mere mode preference but the theologically determined connection between the sign (immersion into water) and the thing signified (burial and resurrection with Christ).

corruption_summary: Believer's baptism has been corrupted by the paedobaptist tradition's application of the sign to the infants of covenant households, collapsing the new covenant's regenerate-only membership criterion into the old covenant's mixed-community pattern — and by the evangelical reduction of baptism to a meaningless social ceremony with no doctrinal weight.
corruption_paragraphs: The paedobaptist argument — that infant baptism is the new covenant equivalent of circumcision, administered on the basis of covenant household membership rather than personal confession — rests on an analogy between the old and new covenant communities that the New Testament does not sustain in the direction paedobaptism requires. Colossians 2:11–12 invokes the circumcision analogy for believer's baptism, not for infant baptism: the “circumcision made without hands” (spiritual regeneration) is the thing to which water baptism corresponds in the passage, and it is accomplished by the Spirit in the heart before the outward sign. The Baptist position is that the new covenant community is explicitly a community whose members “all know me” (Jer 31:34) — inward knowledge that cannot be attributed to an unbaptized infant but only to one the Spirit has regenerated.

The evangelical reduction of baptism to a public testimony — “just a symbol, take it or leave it” — is a different corruption: it evacuates the sign of its enacted gospel-content. The New Testament does not treat baptism as an optional addendum to conversion; it treats it as the first enacted obedience of the new believer, inseparably linked to repentance and faith (Acts 2:38), to union with Christ in death and resurrection (Rom 6:3–4), and to clothing oneself with Christ (Gal 3:27). A theology of baptism as mere public declaration misses the richness of the enacted gospel that Christ designed the sign to convey.
roots_summary: Believer's baptism roots in the new covenant's regenerate-community principle (Jer 31:33–34), in the Acts pattern of confession-before-baptism, in the Pauline theology of baptism as the enacted sign of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, and in the 1689 LBCF as the defining confessional anchor.
roots_lines: Jeremiah 31:33–34 — the new covenant's distinctive: “they shall all know me”; the covenant community is constituted by inward regenerating knowledge, not physical descent — the foundational principle that determines who receives its sign

Acts pattern — Acts 2:38; 8:37–38; 10:44–48; 16:31–33: the consistent apostolic order is believe-and-repent, then be baptized; no counterexample in Acts involves baptism administered to someone who has not first confessed faith

Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12 — baptism as enacted death and resurrection: the sign signifies a spiritual event (dying to the old life; rising in Christ's resurrection) that has already occurred in the regenerate person who receives it

Galatians 3:27 — clothing with Christ: baptism as the public enacted clothing of oneself with Christ, which presupposes that Christ is already possessed by faith; the sign clothes what faith already holds

1689 LBCF 29.1–2 — the confessional anchor: “None are to be baptized but such as do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ”; immersion as the mode fitted to the sign's burial-and-resurrection meaning
usage: The Philip-and-eunuch narrative (Acts 8:26–40) is the paradigmatic believer's baptism account: Scripture reading, gospel explanation, explicit confession of faith (“I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God”), immediate baptism, and the joy that follows. The sequence is not ceremony first and faith later; it is faith operative, then the enacted sign of that faith. The eunuch's joy (Acts 8:39) follows the baptism because the baptism followed and expressed the faith, not as a magical addition to it.

Titus 3:5 — “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit” — uses water-language for regeneration, but the agency is the Spirit (not the water itself). This verse supports the believer's baptism framework: the spiritual washing (regeneration by the Spirit) is the real event; the water baptism is the outward enacted sign of what the Spirit has already accomplished in the regenerate heart.

The paedobaptist-credobaptist debate is a genuine intramural Reformed disagreement, not a salvation issue. The Baptist position of the 1689 LBCF holds that the new covenant's explicitly regenerate membership criterion (Jer 31:34; Heb 8:11) demands a different sign protocol than the old covenant's mixed-community circumcision — and that the Acts pattern of believe-then-baptize is the apostolic settlement of the question.

etymology: Hebrew matstsot (plural of matstsah, unleavened bread or flat bread; root matsats, possibly related to pressing or extracting, or to pressing out the moisture). The term designates bread baked without leaven or yeast — the flat, crackerlike bread eaten during the seven days of the Passover season in obedience to Exodus 12:15–20 and 13:3–10. The Greek rendering is azumos (unleavened), from which Luke 22:1 refers to the “Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover.” The leaven-free character of matzot carries an intentional symbolic weight in Scripture: leaven is consistently used as a type of sin, corruption, and the old nature that is to be purged.
biblical_def: Matzot is the unleavened bread prescribed for the seven-day Passover season beginning the evening of Nisan 14/15 (Exod 12:15–20; Lev 23:5–8; Deut 16:3), eaten in haste by Israel at the Exodus and thereafter as an annual covenant-memorial rehearsal. The command is absolute: “Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread... and no leavened bread shall be seen among you, nor shall any leaven be found among you in all your territory” (Exod 13:7). The unleavened bread carried a double symbolism: it memorialized the speed of the Exodus (there was no time to let bread rise, Exod 12:39) and it enacted the holiness required of those in covenant with the holy God (leaven as type of sin and corruption must be purged from the household). Paul gives the apostolic application in 1 Corinthians 5:7–8: “Christ our Passover also has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast — not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” The purging of physical leaven from Israel's households prefigured the purging of moral leaven from the Christian community. The Lord's Supper itself uses unleavened bread — the matzot of the Passover seder — as the bread Christ broke when He said “this is my body” (Luke 22:1, 7–20). Every matzot cracker in the Supper carries the typological weight of the Passover season's call to purity and the Exodus's call to urgent, delivered haste.
webster_summary: Matzot (matstsot) is the unleavened flat bread prescribed for the Passover season in Exodus 12–13 and Leviticus 23 as a memorial of the Exodus haste and a type of the purging of sin from the covenant community — fulfilled in the New Testament's call to put away the leaven of malice and wickedness (1 Cor 5:7–8).
webster_full: MATZOT. Hebrew matstsot (pl. of matstsah): unleavened flat bread; the bread prescribed for the seven-day Passover season (Nisan 15–21) in Exodus 12:15–20; 13:3–10; Leviticus 23:6–8; eaten by Israel at the Exodus in haste (no time for rising) and thereafter annually as a memorial of the deliverance.

2. The leaven-purging command: no leaven was to be found in any Israelite dwelling during the seven days (Exod 12:15; 13:7); severe covenant sanction for violation (Exod 12:15: “that person shall be cut off from Israel”). The household search and removal of leaven was a physical enacted ritual of covenant holiness.

3. Typological meaning: leaven as the type of sin's pervasive influence (Matt 16:6: “beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees”; 1 Cor 5:6–7: “a little leaven leavens the whole lump”). Matzot, by its absence of leaven, is the type of the holy community purged of the old corrupting nature.

4. New Testament application (1 Cor 5:7–8): “Christ our Passover also has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast — not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” The Passover sacrifice being accomplished, the seven-day holiness the feast demanded is now the permanent character of the Christian community.

5. The Lord's Supper connection: Jesus broke bread at the Passover seder (Luke 22:7–20) — the bread He took was matzot, the Passover unleavened bread. Every observance of the Lord's Supper with unleavened bread carries this typological depth: the bread of haste and deliverance, now the body broken for our sins.

Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread — but on the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses, for whoever eats anything leavened from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel.
Exod 13:7
Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days, and no leavened bread shall be seen among you, nor shall any leaven be found among you in all your territory.
1 Cor 5:7
Clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump — just as you are in fact unleavened. For Christ our Passover also has been sacrificed.
1 Cor 5:8
Therefore let us celebrate the feast — not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
corruption_summary: Matzot has been evacuated of its typological significance in most evangelical practice: the Lord's Supper is often celebrated with leavened bread, and the Passover-season call to communal holiness (“purge out the old leaven”) is treated as Jewish ritual rather than as the New Testament's own model for church discipline and regenerate community life.
corruption_paragraphs: The widespread evangelical use of leavened bread in the Lord's Supper is not a salvation-level issue, but it quietly severs the typological connection that Paul explicitly draws in 1 Corinthians 5:7–8. When Paul says “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us celebrate the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth,” he is applying the Passover matzot-purge to the church's practice of removing the leavened sinner from its midst (1 Cor 5:1–6). The physical type (unleavened bread at Passover) and the apostolic application (purge out the leavened man; celebrate with sincerity and truth) are a connected argument. Recovering matzot's typological weight means recovering the church discipline imperative that Paul draws from it.

The historical-critical dismissal of the matzot regulations as late Priestly legislation imposed on an older nomadic shepherd festival destroys the typological intentionality the New Testament assumes. If the unleavened bread requirement is a Second Temple-era addition rather than Mosaic law, Paul's typological application in 1 Corinthians 5 loses its grounding: how can the leaven-purge of Exodus 12 be a type of the church's discipline if Exodus 12 was itself only composed in the post-exilic period? The Reformed answer is that the Mosaic authenticity of the Passover legislation is the foundation of Paul's typological argument — deny the former and the latter collapses.
roots_summary: Matzot roots in the Exodus night's urgent departure (no time for rising bread, Exod 12:39), in the seven-day Passover season's enacted holiness-demand (no leaven in any dwelling), and in the New Testament's apostolic extension of the leaven-purge metaphor to the Christian community's call to live as an unleavened holy congregation.
roots_lines: Exodus 12:39 — the historical origin: the Israelites baked unleavened cakes because they were thrust out of Egypt suddenly and could not wait for the dough to rise; urgency and deliverance are baked into the bread from the first moment

Exodus 12:15–20; 13:3–10 — the covenant legislation: leaven to be utterly purged from the household for seven days; the severity of the sanction (“cut off from Israel”) reflects how seriously God treats the holiness-type

Leaven as sin-type — Matt 16:6, 11–12; 1 Cor 5:6–7: Jesus uses leaven for false teaching; Paul uses leaven for the pervasive corrupting power of tolerated sin in the church; both treatments assume the established Passover typology

First Corinthians 5:7–8 — the apostolic application: since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the seven-day matzot-festival of holiness is now the permanent character of the Christian community; purge out the leavened man; feast with unleavened sincerity and truth

Lord's Supper connection — Luke 22:7–20: the bread Jesus took at the Last Supper was the Passover unleavened bread; matzot is the original substance of the Supper's bread element, carrying the full weight of the Passover typology into every Christian observance of it
usage: First Corinthians 5:7–8 makes the matzot typology the foundation of Paul's church-discipline argument: the incestuous man must be removed (“purge out the old leaven”) precisely because the church is an unleavened community for whom the Passover Lamb has been sacrificed. Church discipline is not a harsh optional extra; it is the matzot-logic applied to the living congregation. A church that tolerates visible unrepentant sin is a leavened Passover feast — an internal contradiction.

The urgency baked into matzot — the bread of hasty departure, eaten with sandals on and staff in hand (Exod 12:11) — speaks to the Christian life's pilgrim character. The redeemed do not settle into Egypt; they eat in haste, dressed for departure, as those who belong to another country. The matzot-eating discipline of the Passover season is an annual enacted reminder that the church is always on the move, not at home in the present age.

The leaven/matzot contrast of 1 Corinthians 5:8 — “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” versus “the leaven of malice and wickedness” — defines the texture of authentic Christian community. Sincerity (eilikrinēia, purity tested by sunlight) and truth (alētheia, unhiddenness, reality) are the positive unleavened qualities that matzot represents in the moral life of the assembly. These are not natural virtues; they are the fruit of a community whose Passover Lamb has been slain and whose leaven has been purged.

etymology: Feast (from Latin festum, festival day, celebration) + unleavened (from Old English: prefix un- + leavened, from Old French levain, leaven, fermented dough, from Latin levamen, something that raises) + bread (Old English brēad, piece, morsel, leavened loaf). The Hebrew is Chag HaMatzot (“feast of the unleavened breads”): the seven-day festival immediately following Passover (Nisan 15–21) during which Israel ate no leavened bread. Luke 22:1 uses “Feast of Unleavened Bread” and “Passover” interchangeably, as the two had become fused in common usage by the New Testament era.
biblical_def: The Feast of Unleavened Bread (Chag HaMatzot) is the seven-day covenant festival commanded by God in Exodus 12:15–20 and Leviticus 23:6–8, beginning on the fifteenth of Nisan the day after Passover and continuing through the twenty-first. During these seven days all leaven was to be utterly removed from Israelite dwellings and all bread eaten was to be the flat, unleavened matzot. The feast memorialized both the Exodus haste (Israel left Egypt so suddenly there was no time for bread to rise, Exod 12:39) and the holiness demanded of the covenant people (leaven as the type of corruption and sin's pervasive spread). The first and seventh days were designated holy convocations (Lev 23:7–8) with no customary work permitted. The entire festival was one of the three pilgrimage feasts at which all Israelite males appeared before the LORD at the central sanctuary (Deut 16:16: “the Feast of Unleavened Bread” heading the list). Leviticus 23:6 gives the timing: “And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Festival of Unleavened Bread to the LORD; for seven days you must eat unleavened bread.” Exodus 12:17 grounds it in the Exodus event: “You shall also observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread — for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt.” The apostle Paul's application in 1 Corinthians 5:7–8 transforms the seven-day matzot-festival into a permanent moral category for the church: since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the church is to be an unleavened community, purging out the old leaven of malice and celebrating the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
webster_summary: The Feast of Unleavened Bread (Chag HaMatzot, Lev 23:6–8) is the seven-day Passover-season festival in which Israel removed all leaven from their homes and ate only unleavened bread — memorializing the Exodus haste and enacting the covenant holiness demanded of the redeemed people of God.
webster_full: FEAST OF UNLEAVENED BREAD. Hebrew Chag HaMatzot: the seven-day festival (Nisan 15–21) commanded in Exodus 12:15–20; Leviticus 23:6–8; Deuteronomy 16:3–8, immediately following Passover; all leaven to be purged from Israelite homes; only unleavened flat bread (matzot) to be eaten.

2. Dual commemoration: (a) the Exodus haste — Israel fled Egypt before their bread could rise (Exod 12:39), so the unleavened bread memorializes the deliverance itself; (b) the covenant holiness — the leaven-free household is an enacted declaration that the redeemed community has been separated from Egypt's corruption and belongs wholly to the holy God.

3. Prescribed holy convocations: the first day (Nisan 15) and seventh day (Nisan 21) were sacred assemblies with no ordinary work (Lev 23:7–8); the entire seven-day span was an elevated season of covenant self-examination and separation from leaven.

4. Pilgrimage requirement: the Feast of Unleavened Bread headed the list of the three mandatory annual pilgrimages to the central sanctuary (Deut 16:16; Exod 23:15; 34:18); every Israelite male was to appear before the LORD with an offering proportional to his blessing.

5. New Testament fulfillment (1 Cor 5:7–8): since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the seven-day matzot-festival becomes the permanent moral posture of the church — purging out the leavened man (church discipline, 1 Cor 5:2–5) and celebrating the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

You shall also observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread — for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this day throughout your generations as a permanent ordinance.
Lev 23:6
And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Festival of Unleavened Bread to the LORD; for seven days you must eat unleavened bread.
Luke 22:1
Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover, was approaching.
1 Cor 5:8
Therefore let us celebrate the feast — not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
corruption_summary: The Feast of Unleavened Bread has been corrupted by historical-critical reduction to a Canaanite agricultural borrowing and by evangelical neglect of the feast's church-discipline imperative that Paul draws from it in 1 Corinthians 5 — so that churches celebrate the Passover season without ever purging out the leaven of tolerated sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical source analysis treats Chag HaMatzot as a pre-Mosaic Canaanite spring agricultural festival (festival of barley harvest, celebrated with unleavened bread because the new grain had not yet fermented) that was later historicized by the Exodus narrative and attached to Passover by a post-exilic scribal editor. This framework denies the Mosaic institution and the typological intentionality of the leaven-purge. The Reformed confessional position holds that Exodus 12's legislation is exactly what it claims: the LORD's own command at Sinai, grounded in the specific historical circumstances of the Exodus night and designed from its institution to be a type of the covenant community's holiness before the holy God.

The evangelical church's loss of the feast's church-discipline content is the more immediate practical corruption. First Corinthians 5 is Paul's most explicit statement about church discipline, and it is structured as a Passover-season typological argument: you are unleavened (the Lamb has been slain); therefore purge out the leavened man (exercise discipline); celebrate the feast with unleavened sincerity and truth. Churches that practice no meaningful discipline have abandoned the matzot-logic at the very point Paul most directly applies it. The tolerated leaven — the unrepentant, openly sinning member welcomed to the Lord's Table — is precisely what the Feast of Unleavened Bread was designed to end.
roots_summary: The Feast of Unleavened Bread roots in the Exodus night's hasty departure (Exod 12:39), in the Mosaic covenant legislation of Exodus 12–13 and Leviticus 23, and in the New Testament's apostolic extension of the leaven-purge to the church's permanent moral call to be an unleavened holy community.
roots_lines: Exodus 12:15–20; 13:3–10 — the original legislation: seven days of leaven-free bread; severe covenant sanction for leavened eating; the feast named and grounded in the Exodus deliverance
Leviticus 23:6–8 — the feast codified in the covenant calendar: the fifteenth of Nisan as the feast's formal beginning; first and seventh days as holy convocations; no ordinary work
Deuteronomy 16:3–8 — the pilgrimage dimension: the bread of affliction eaten “in haste”; the seven-day feast at the central sanctuary; the morning release and return after seven days

First Corinthians 5:6–8 — the New Testament typological application: Christ's sacrifice as the Passover slaughter; the church as an unleavened community; the leaven-purge as church discipline; the feast-celebration as sincerity and truth

Luke 22:1 — the Passover-Unleavened Bread fusion: by the first century the Feast of Unleavened Bread and Passover were practically synonymous in common usage; Jesus' Last Supper occurs within this combined season and is the fulfillment of both
usage: Exodus 12:17 grounds the feast in the historical specificity of the Exodus: “on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt.” The feast is not a general religious observance about purity; it is a commemoration of a specific dated redemptive act. This historical groundedness prevents the feast's moral demands (no leaven, holiness) from becoming abstract moralism: they are the response of a specific people to a specific divine deliverance. The church's call to holiness is similarly grounded in the specific, dated, historical sacrifice of the Passover Lamb on the cross.

The fusion of Passover and Unleavened Bread in New Testament usage (Luke 22:1: “the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover”) shows that by the first century these two festivals were experienced as a continuous eight-day arc from the Passover sacrifice to the end of the unleavened-bread season. The theological logic is sound: the sacrifice (Passover) and the holiness it demands (seven days of no leaven) belong together. You cannot celebrate the sacrifice while tolerating the corruption.

The two holy convocations of the feast — the first day (Nisan 15) and seventh day (Nisan 21) — bracket the entire seven-day period with sacred assemblies. The church's regular Lord's Day gatherings bookend weeks in the same way: the community gathers to begin each week in the Lord's presence and lives out the week as an unleavened community before gathering again. The seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread is a type of the Christian week.

etymology: Cup (Old English cuppe, from Latin cuppa, tub or cask; by extension, the drinking vessel and its contents) + blessing (Old English blētsian, to consecrate by blood or to invoke divine favor). The phrase “cup of blessing” translates Greek to potērion tēs eulogías of 1 Corinthians 10:16, where Paul designates the Lord's Supper cup with the same term used in the Passover seder for the third cup of the Passover service — the cup drunk after the meal, over which a blessing was pronounced. The cup's Passover-seder background is the wine over which Jesus spoke the words of institution at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20: “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood”).
biblical_def: The cup of blessing is the consecrated cup of the Lord's Supper — the cup Paul identifies in 1 Corinthians 10:16 as “a sharing in the blood of Christ,” the vehicle through which the gathered church participates in the covenant sealed by Christ's poured-out blood. Paul's question is rhetorical: “Is not the cup of blessing which we bless a sharing in the blood of Christ?” The answer is yes — the cup genuinely participates in what it signifies and enacts, not in a Roman sacramental sense (transubstantiation), but in the Reformed sense that the Spirit genuinely feeds the faith of believing participants through the cup's enacted gospel-content. The cup of blessing at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20) is the Passover's third cup — the cup of redemption drunk after the Passover meal. Jesus takes this cup and identifies it with the new covenant in His blood: “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood.” Matthew 26:27–28 records His words of institution: “Drink from it, all of you. For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins.” The cup thus becomes the covenant-renewal instrument of the new covenant, the enacted proclamation of the shed blood that ratified the covenant at Calvary. Hebrews 9:20 quotes Exodus 24:8 (“This is the blood of the covenant”) in reference to the Mosaic covenant-inauguration at Sinai — establishing the typological lineage: Sinai blood on the people, cross blood in the cup. Every Supper cup carries this covenant-inaugurating weight.
webster_summary: The cup of blessing is the consecrated Lord's Supper cup identified by Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:16 as a genuine sharing in Christ's blood — the enacted proclamation of the new covenant ratified by Christ's shed blood, rooted in the Passover seder's third cup and fulfilled in Jesus' words of institution at the Last Supper.
webster_full: CUP OF BLESSING. Greek to potērion tēs eulogías (1 Cor 10:16): the consecrated cup of the Lord's Supper, over which a blessing is pronounced, identified by Paul as a genuine participation (koinōnia) in the blood of Christ.

2. Passover-seder background: the third of four Passover cups (“the cup of redemption” in rabbinic tradition), drunk after the Passover meal over which a blessing was pronounced. Jesus takes this cup at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20) and redefines its content: no longer the covenant blood of the Exodus redemption, but the new covenant blood of His own self-offering.

3. Words of institution (Matt 26:27–28): “Drink from it, all of you. For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins.” The cup is the new covenant's covenant-meal instrument, the blood of the covenant enacted in the drinking community.

4. The Reformed understanding: koinōnia (sharing/participation) in 1 Cor 10:16 is a real spiritual participation mediated by the Spirit through faith — not transubstantiation (the cup literally becomes blood) and not bare memorialism (the cup signifies nothing present); the Spirit genuinely feeds believing participants through the cup's enacted gospel-content.

5. Covenant-blood typology (Exod 24:8; Heb 9:20): Moses sprinkled blood on the people at Sinai saying “this is the blood of the covenant.” The cup of blessing is the new covenant's equivalent: Christ's blood applied to the covenant community not by sprinkling but by the cup's proclaiming and the faith's receiving.

And when He had taken a cup and given thanks, He gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you.

And in the same way He took the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood.
corruption_summary: The cup of blessing has been corrupted by Roman Catholic transubstantiation (the cup literally becomes Christ's blood through priestly consecration) and by Protestant sacramentarian memorialism (the cup is a bare symbol with no genuine spiritual participation in what it enacts) — both positions failing Paul's declared koinōnia (real participation) in 1 Corinthians 10:16.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman Catholic eucharistic theology teaches that through transubstantiation the cup's substance is converted into Christ's actual blood at the moment of priestly consecration. This position collapses the sign-and-thing-signified distinction that the Reformation recovered: the cup is the sign; the blood of Christ is the thing signified; the Spirit genuinely mediates the latter through the former to the faith of the believing participant, but the former does not literally become the latter. The Council of Trent anathematized the Reformed view; the Westminster Confession (29.6) and the 1689 LBCF (30.7) reject transubstantiation as repugnant to Scripture, overthrow the nature of the ordinance, and have been productive of much superstition.

The Zwinglian-sacramentarian reduction goes too far in the opposite direction: the cup is merely a memorial token, a symbol pointing to an absent Christ and his past work, with no genuine present participation mediated through it. First Corinthians 10:16 refuses this reduction: koinōnia in Paul's vocabulary is a genuine present sharing, not a commemorative gesture. The Reformed position (Calvin, the Westminster Standards, the 1689 LBCF) is that Christ is genuinely present to the faith of believers at the Supper through the Spirit's mediation — the cup is a genuine means of grace, not a mere memorial, even though Christ's body is in heaven and the cup contains wine.
roots_summary: The cup of blessing roots in the Passover seder's third cup (the cup of redemption), in Moses' covenant-blood-sprinkling at Sinai (Exod 24:8), in Christ's words of institution at the Last Supper, and in Paul's apostolic definition of the Supper cup as genuine koinōnia in the blood of Christ.
roots_lines: Passover seder third cup — “the cup of redemption”: the cup Jesus takes after the meal (Luke 22:20: “after they had eaten”) is the third Passover cup; its Exodus-redemption content is now reinterpreted by Jesus as the new-covenant blood ratification

Exodus 24:8 — covenant-blood typology: Moses sprinkles blood on the people at Sinai declaring “this is the blood of the covenant”; Jesus echoes this formula exactly at the Last Supper (Matt 26:28: “this is my blood of the covenant”), establishing the new covenant's blood-ratification in fulfillment of the old

Matthew 26:27–28 — words of institution: the cup given to all participants; the blood poured out for many; the forgiveness of sins as the cup's covenant-content; the Supper as the new covenant's ongoing ratification-meal

First Corinthians 10:16 — Paul's definition: koinōnia (genuine participation, sharing, communion) in Christ's blood; the cup of blessing is not a bare memorial but a Spirit-mediated real participation in the atonement's benefit

Hebrews 9:20 — the typological lineage: Hebrews quotes Exod 24:8 to describe the Sinai covenant's blood-sprinkling as the type; the antitype is Christ's blood applied through the cup of blessing to the new covenant community
usage: First Corinthians 10:16's koinōnia language makes the cup of blessing the primary New Testament text for understanding the Lord's Supper's spiritual character. The cup is not a bare reminder of something that happened once; it is a genuine present participation in the covenant benefit secured by Christ's blood. The believing participant at the Supper is not merely remembering Calvary from a distance; through the Spirit's mediation he or she is genuinely receiving the covenant benefit that Calvary secured.

Luke 22:20's declaration — “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in My blood” — is the Supper's covenant-renewal charter. Every Supper is a covenant-renewal act: the church gathered around the cup of blessing is re-ratifying its covenant relationship with the God who poured out Christ's blood for its redemption. The Supper is not a ceremony with no ongoing covenant significance; it is the new covenant's regular covenant-renewal meal.

The communal character of the cup — “Drink from it, all of you” (Matt 26:27) — makes the cup of blessing an act of covenant solidarity. Paul extends this in 1 Corinthians 10:17: “Since there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread.” The cup creates and declares a unity among its participants as sharers in the one blood; to drink it in an unworthy manner (1 Cor 11:27–29) is to make a false covenant claim about belonging to the body of Christ.

etymology: Blood (Old English blod, the vital fluid; in biblical usage, the carrier of life, Lev 17:11) + of the covenant (from Old French covenant, agreement, treaty, from Latin convenire). The phrase “blood of the covenant” translates Hebrew dam haberit (Exod 24:8; Zech 9:11) and Greek haima tēs diathēkēs (Matt 26:28; Heb 9:20). In biblical covenantal theology, covenants are ratified by blood: the slaughter of animals and the application of their blood to the covenant parties (the covenant-cutting ritual of Gen 15) or to the covenant community (the Sinai blood-sprinkling of Exod 24) seals the covenant's binding force. Blood ratification thus signifies both life-oath (“may I die like this animal if I break this covenant”) and life-gift (the life of the sacrifice poured out in the covenant's inauguration).
biblical_def: The blood of the covenant is the atoning, ratifying blood that seals the binding relationship between God and His people — in type, the blood of sacrificial animals at Sinai (Exod 24:8); in antitype and fulfillment, the blood of Jesus Christ poured out at Calvary for the ratification of the new covenant (Matt 26:28; Heb 9:20). Exodus 24:8 records the Sinai ratification: Moses took the blood of young bulls sacrificed as burnt offerings and peace offerings, “sprinkled it on the people, and said, 'This is the blood of the covenant which the LORD has made with you according to all these words.'” The blood was first sprinkled on the altar (representing God's side) and then on the people — a bilateral act of covenant-sealing that bound both parties to the covenant's terms. Hebrews 9:20 quotes Exodus 24:8 in its discussion of the superiority of Christ's priestly work, establishing the typological lineage: the Sinai blood pointed forward to a better blood. Zechariah 9:11 announces the covenant-blood as the ground of liberation: “As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit.” The new covenant's blood is Christ's own blood: Matthew 26:28 records His words of institution at the Last Supper, “For this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins.” Hebrews 13:20 calls Christ's blood “the blood of the eternal covenant,” establishing its permanent, unrepeatable, eternally valid character. The blood of the covenant is the ground of every covenant benefit: justification, forgiveness, adoption, sanctification, and final glorification all rest on this poured-out blood.
webster_summary: The blood of the covenant is the atoning, ratifying blood that seals God's covenant with His people — in type, the Sinai blood-sprinkling of Exodus 24:8; in fulfillment, the blood of Jesus Christ poured out for the forgiveness of sins (Matt 26:28) and the ratification of the new covenant.
webster_full: BLOOD OF THE COVENANT. Hebrew dam haberit; Greek haima tēs diathēkēs: the blood by which a covenant is ratified and sealed, applied to the covenant parties as the binding oath-sacrifice that inaugurates the covenant relationship.

2. Sinai ratification (Exod 24:3–8): Moses reads the Book of the Covenant; the people confess covenant allegiance; animals are sacrificed; blood is divided — half sprinkled on the altar (God's side) and half sprinkled on the people (Israel's side); Moses declares “this is the blood of the covenant.” The covenant is doubly ratified by blood touching both parties.

3. Covenantal blood-ratification theology: in the ancient Near Eastern treaty pattern (and in the Abrahamic covenant of Gen 15), animals are slaughtered and the parties pass between them, invoking the oath: “may I become like these animals if I break this covenant.” At Sinai, God graciously binds Himself with Israel through blood rather than requiring Israel alone to pass between the pieces.

4. Christ's words of institution (Matt 26:28): “this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for forgiveness of sins” — the Sinai formula echoed and surpassed; the better blood of the better covenant (Heb 9:23; 12:24) ratifying the eternal covenant between God and His elect in Christ.

5. The blood's covenant-benefits: Hebrews 13:20–21 prays through “the blood of the eternal covenant” for sanctification; Zechariah 9:11 grounds liberation from captivity in the covenant-blood; Revelation 12:11 describes the overcomers conquering “by the blood of the Lamb.” Every covenant benefit flows from the poured-out blood.

Heb 9:20
saying, “This is the blood of the covenant which God commanded you.”
